paras: The threatened lynching of Ernest Blakeney occurred on July 9, 1903, near O. K. in Lancaster County, South Carolina, when a crowd gathered to hunt down a 19-year-old Black farm hand accused of climbing into the bedroom window of his employer's daughter. After the crowd agreed that he ought to be killed, men among it, including the young woman's father and brother, persuaded it to hand him to the sheriff. South Carolina papers praised the county for letting the law take its course, and in October Blakeney was sentenced to life imprisonment for burglary.

Blakeney, described by the Lancaster Ledger as "a negro about 19 years of age," was hired to J. H. Stewart of O. K. and sometimes slept in a cabin on Stewart's plantation. A special correspondent of The State placed the Stewart home in "the Tabernacle section" of the county and called Stewart "a prominent citizen."

According to the Ledger, at about 2 a.m. on Thursday a man stacked two boxes beneath the window of Stewart's daughter and climbed in, but his foot landed on a trunk on rollers, the noise woke her, and he fled when she screamed. The Newberry Herald and News named her as Miss Dassie Stewart and placed the incident on "Wednesday night." The Ledger said she recognized Blakeney in the bright moonlight, and that while her father watched the cabin, her brother, Rochel Stewart, telephoned the neighbors.

By daylight a crowd had gathered at the Stewart place to join the search, and Blakeney walked into the yard. The papers reported that he first denied the charge and then confessed; The State's correspondent added that he said "he had been put up to it by other negroes." The Ledger wrote that a lynching then "seemed imminent" and that all present, Black people included, agreed "the brute ought to be killed."

The Ledger credited Abel Funderburk, J. H. Stewart and Rochel Stewart with persuading the crowd "to let the law take its course." Rochel Stewart, Funderburk and B. B. Plyler then took Blakeney to town and turned him over to the sheriff, and he was committed on a charge of entering a dwelling at night "with the intent to commit an unmentionable crime."

At the October 1903 term of court in Lancaster, Blakeney was sentenced to life imprisonment in the penitentiary for burglary, and a penitentiary guard then took him to Columbia. The coverage does not describe the trial itself, and no one in the crowd was reported charged.

The Ledger ran its account under the headline "A Negro Enters the Window of A Lady's Room-Cool Heads Prevented Lynching," calling Blakeney "the brute" and "the miserable wretch" while praising the "law-abiding men" who "saved that negro's neck." It commended the O. K. people for submitting "to the majesty of the law when the ends of justice would seemingly have been more speedily met by the rule of the mob." The Lancaster Enterprise printed the same text under the same headline on July 15, and the Yorkville Enquirer reprinted it that day among items from neighboring papers.

The State's Lancaster special, carried as "Trusting to the Law" by the Batesburg Advocate and the Manning Times on July 15, set the county's "law abiding spirit" against "the spirit of lawlessness which prevails in other portions of the United States." In an editorial paragraph, the Yorkville Enquirer called the accused a "Negro fiend" and said the incident reflected "the highest credit on Lancaster county," above all on R. S. Stewart, who "stood for the law under such terrible provocation." The Newberry paper's brief, which the Anderson Intelligencer reprinted on July 22, likewise said the lynching was prevented "only by the efforts" of the brother.
All of the coverage came from white South Carolina weeklies, which treated Blakeney's guilt as settled and the crowd's restraint as the news; no Black-press account was found.

The accounts differ in detail: the Ledger said he was jailed Thursday morning and only put a foot inside the room, while The State's correspondent said he was brought to jail Friday and had entered the room before the young woman woke; they also credit different men with calming the crowd.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Ernest Blakeney
bases: A crowd gathered to hunt an accused Black man, agreed he 'ought to be killed' and proposed to 'make short work of him', but was persuaded to hand him to the sheriff; a threatened lynching (A1, A3).

A crowd (3+) threatened to kill Blakeney over an accusation of entering a young white woman's room, but no killing occurred: he was delivered alive to the sheriff and later sentenced in court (A1, A3, A9). It is a threatened, not a completed, lynching.

The Lancaster Ledger's local account (A1) and The State's separate Lancaster special (A3) agree on the window entry, the crowd's intent to kill, and the handover to the sheriff; the Newberry brief (A2) adds the young woman's name and also reports a prevented lynching.

accounts.label: Lancaster Ledger (local)
accounts.gist: Blakeney climbed into the daughter's window, fled when she screamed, walked into the yard at daylight, confessed; the crowd agreed he should be killed until law-abiding men prevailed on it to let the law act.

accounts.label: The State's Lancaster correspondent
accounts.gist: He had entered the room before she woke; it was 'proposed to make short work of him' but the father advised jail; he confessed and said other Black men had put him up to it; brought to jail Friday.

accounts.label: Newberry Herald and News
accounts.gist: Miss Dassie Stewart found a man trying to enter her room on Wednesday night; Blakeney confessed; her brother R. S. Stewart alone prevented a lynching.

framing.detail: The Ledger opposed the lynching and praised the 'law-abiding men' who 'saved that negro's neck', while calling Blakeney 'the brute' and 'the miserable wretch' and treating his guilt as settled.
The State's special, headed 'Trusting to the Law', contrasted the county's 'law abiding spirit' with lawlessness elsewhere in the United States.
The Yorkville Enquirer editorial praised R. S. Stewart for standing 'for the law under such terrible provocation' and called the accused a 'Negro fiend'.

conflicts.note: The Ledger is the local paper and gives a detailed timeline; The State's special may be loose on the day.

quotes: When asked his motive he told of his evil purpose in entering the room and it was then for awhile that a lynching seemed imminent.
Feeling became intense, not even the people of his own race who were there having any feeling for him, all agreeing that the brute ought to be killed.
We cannot commend the O. K. people too highly that they have submitted to the majesty of the law when the ends of justice would seemingly have been more speedily met by the rule of the mob.
